prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for its first experimental realization with protected edge states in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: The Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a genuinely new organising principle for electronic band structure: topology of the occupied bands, not symmetry breaking, fixes the character of the phase. The idea is original and conceptually clean, it was realised in HgTe wells within about a year of the proposal, and it has been confirmed across many material families (HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi-based compounds, three-dimensional topological insulators by ARPES). It has also changed practice in my own area: systematic first-principles searches for topological materials and the calculation of topological invariants are now routine parts of electronic-structure work. Roughly two decades of independent confirmation make this mature, and the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and the Haldane-type models rather than this line, so the recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weak point. The three supplied names do not capture the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp's group where to look in HgTe, nor Fu, Kane and Mele (and Moore, Balents, Roy) for the three-dimensional generalisation, nor the experimental ARPES work. Any three-person prize will be contested on who is left out. The statement of the achievement is also open to being framed more narrowly (the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect) or more broadly (all topological insulators), and its overlap with the quantum anomalous Hall candidate I saw earlier in the longlist is unresolved. Finally, the headline technological promise of dissipationless edge transport has not materialised, so the case rests on conceptual and scientific influence rather than applications.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B006) first as a prediction followed by a nature-led experimental surprise, and puts B055 second, noting that its credit allocation is contested.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is a strong discovery-centred case and I ranked it second myself, but I weigh maturity differently. The origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated insulators in twisted bilayer graphene is still debated, so the citation would have to be written around observation rather than understanding, and the field is only about eight years old. B055 carries the same prediction-plus-experiment structure with a stable, universally accepted interpretation. I accept his point about attribution for B055 and share it, but the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction also has precursors (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell), so contested credit is not a differentiator in favour of B006. I would take B006 in a later year once the correlated phases are better understood.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B015) first as a clean, original advance in precision measurement, confirmed in many laboratories, with a two-person credit of Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I ranked B015 last of my eight, which says more about my distance from atomic metrology than about its quality, and Kroll and Lindroth have persuaded me that it is a first-rate invention with a clean two-person credit; I now treat it as my second alternative. My reservations are specific rather than dismissive: the redefinition of the second is still pending, and the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes cover neighbouring ground, so the citation must be framed around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation. I do not think those reservations outweigh the fact that the condensed-matter candidates reach us with larger attribution problems. If the committee wants a configuration with the cleanest credit, B015 beats B055 and I would not oppose it, but I do not think it exceeds B055 in scientific reach.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class (B023) first, arguing that a stochastic-dynamics idea became a precise, testable universal theory, with Kardar, Zhang and Takeuchi as the supportable trio.
responses.response: I find the KPZ case intellectually attractive, and I recognise that the equation defines a real universality class. My difficulty is the same one Mehlig identifies: the most striking modern content, the exact solutions and the Tracy-Widom statistics, comes from mathematical physicists who are not in the supplied credit, so a prize to Kardar, Zhang and Takeuchi would reward the 1986 equation plus one experiment rather than the part of the story that made it precise. That is a harder attribution problem than B055, where the credited names do cover the prediction and the first realisation, even if others are omitted. I would want the committee to see whether a citation limited to the equation and its experimental confirmation is defensible before I support it over B055.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B024) first as the clearest foundational step beyond the circuit physics honoured in 2025, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf and a very mature experimental record.
responses.response: The maturity argument is sound and I do not dispute the scientific importance of circuit QED. Where I qualify his view is the 2025 overlap: that prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and awarding a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon, in a closely related subject, is something the committee should justify rather than assume. Johansson also flags that his own subfield proximity affects his view of the credit split, and Girvin's role in both the 2004 proposal and the transmon is a real attribution gap among the supplied names. I treat B024 as a serious candidate but not as my first choice, and I did not include it among my alternatives for those two reasons.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle on a defensible three-person credit for B055 given that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and others fall outside the supplied names.
Whether the citation should be framed narrowly around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect or broadly around topological insulators, and how that interacts with other topological candidates.
Whether B006 will be judged mature enough, given the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity and correlated states in twisted bilayer graphene.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work is in electronic-structure theory and magnetism and I use methods related to topological-materials calculations, but my profile documents no personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, or the other credited names on the shortlist.
